newsitem.title: UK: UK gilt supply pressure off as CGBR set to dip.
newsitem.headline: UK gilt supply pressure off as CGBR set to dip.

text.p: The UK gilt market could be looking at the lowest level of supply for six years in fiscal 1997-98, reflecting an expected reduction in required government borrowing and a sizeable overfund from 1996-97, analysts say.

The picture for conventional gilts is even brighter because the government has pledged to increase the proportion of bonds which pay a fixed return over retail price inflation -- index-linked gilts -- it sells to 20 percent of total issuance.

The authorities are hoping this increase from 15 percent of the total will increase the liquidity of the index-linked market, but it will also have the knock-on effect of trimming conventional issuance.
"Whatever else the gilt market has to worry about -- and I can think of a number of problems -- funding is not one of them," said Morgan Stanley UK economist Kevin Gardiner.
The UK government bond market is currently beset by worries about rising interest rates, the May 1 election and concerns that inflation may be set to increase again.
The Bank of England has to issue enough gilts to cover the Central Government Borrowing Requirement (CGBR) as well as redemptions of maturing government bonds.
With redemptions set to soar to their highest level ever at 20 billion stg in the current fiscal year, from 12.5 billion in fiscal 1996-97, supply has been a niggling worry.
But analysts say the nervousness is misplaced.
"The government has a very easy funding task this year," said Brian Hilliard, chief economist at Societe Generale's fixed income division.

Instead of the 20 billion stg predicted at the November budget, the deficit is likely to come in at between 13.0 and 19.1 billion, analysts say. This will result in a comparable reduction of the amount of gilts which need to be sold.
But the authorities are also carrying forward an overfund of 3.9 billion stg from fiscal 1996-97, according to the Bank of England, and this will also cut required gilt issuance.

The 1996-97 overfund stems from a combination of a lower than expected CGBR for the year -- 25.1 billion stg instead of the official forecast of 27.9 billion -- a fall in the level of official reserves of foreign currency and 0.2 billion stg more than expected in sales of National Savings products.

HSBC economist Don Smith has one of the most bullish forecasts for the level of gilt issuance this year, arguing gross sales of gilts will be just 25.0 billion stg, the lowest level since 1991-92 when sales totalled 18.1 billion.
In fiscal 1996-97, gross gilt sales were 38.9 billion.
Smith expects 20 billion stg of the gilts sold in the current fiscal year to be conventionals, down from 33.0 billion in fiscal 1996-97 and the lowest level since 16.8 billion in 1991-92.
Sales of index-linked gilts will come to 5.0 billion stg, down from 5.9 billion in fiscal 1996-97.
"We think the gilt market has yet to come to terms with the prospect of a sharp squeeze in conventional gilt issuance in the coming financial year," Smith said.
"If our forecast proves right, the auction calendar will have to be adjusted to accommodate a lower level of gilt sales."

Smith's forecast assumes that the next government puts in place a 4.0 billion stg fiscal tightening package, but even if this does not occur, auction sizes are still likely to be on the low side, he said.

"If there is no fiscal tightening at all, this would change our conventional gilt sales estimate to 24 billion stg, still lower than the 26 billion stg minimum accommodated by the current auction schedule," he said.
The Bank of England has planned 11 auctions in the current fiscal year.
Four of these will involve two stocks at a time. The auction size can range from 2.0 to 3.0 billion stg for single stock auctions and from 3.0 to 4.5 billion for the dual ones.
The Bank can also raise funds through less formal tap sales.

Morgan Stanley's Gardiner is slightly less bullish, seeing gross gilt sales of around 28.0 billion stg, but this would still be the lowest figure since 1991-92. He is looking for a CGBR of around 17.0 billion compared with HSBC's 13.0 billion.
Societe Generale sees gross issuance of some 33.0 billion stg while Goldman Sachs economist David Walton is forecasting around 32 billion and BZW's Kevin Adams foresees 35.1 billion.

Adams expects the CGBR to come in at around 22 billion stg, arguing that the next government, of whichever party, is unlikely to be able to meet the stringent spending targets set by the Conservatives and accepted by Labour.
"You have to worry that some of the assumptions on spending are somewhat ambitious. Growth of just 1/2 percent in real terms has never been achieved," he said.
If the funding bulls are right, then the UK government bond market has a cushion against the climate of rising bond yields internationally.
"Net funding is going to fall very sharply but this will restrain rising yields, rather than turn a bear market into a bull one," Morgan Stanley's Gardiner said.
